INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
Constitutional Accountability Center (CAC) is a
think tank and public  interest law firm dedicated to
fulfilling the progressive promise of the Constitution’s
text and history.  CAC works in our courts, through
our government, and with legal scholars to improve
understanding of the Constitution and to preserve the
rights and freedoms it guarantees.  CAC has a strong
interest in ensuring meaningful access to the courts,
in accordance with constitutional text and history, and
accordingly has an interest in this case.
INTRODUCTION AND
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Kekai Watanabe was “brutally” attacked in a fight
at a Honolulu federal prison  and “sustained severe
injuries,” including a broken coccyx.  Pet. App. 2a , 4a.
He presented at sick call with “severe back pain” and
“known and visible injuries” and requested medical
attention.  Id. at 4a.  Francis Nielsen, a federal prison
nurse, told him “to stop being a cry baby.”  Id.  Nielsen
refused to send Watanabe to a hospital  or to provide
any medical care besides “over -the-counter pain
medication.”  Id.  When Watanabe finally received an
x-ray seven months later, the scan revealed that his
coccyx was in fact  broken and that  pieces of it had
“migrated and entered the surrounding soft tissue.”
Id.

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part,
and no counsel or party made a monetary contribution intended
to fund its preparation or submission.  No person other than
amicus or its counsel made a monetary contribution to its
preparation or submission.

2

Watanabe subsequently sued Nielsen seeking
money damages to redress Nielsen’s deliberate
indifference to his serious injuries.  The Constitution’s
text and history make plain that he can bring this suit
because individuals can sue in a court of law to hold
federal officers accountable for violating their
constitutionally guaranteed rights, as this Court held
in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal
Bureau of Narcotics , 403 U.S. 388 (1971) .  There,
recognizing that “damages have been regarded as the
ordinary remedy for an invasion of personal interests
in liberty ,” id. at 395,  this Court “vindicate[d] the
Constitution by allowing some redress for injuries ,”
Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120, 134 (2017); see Bivens,
403 U.S. at 395 (holding that “damages may be
obtained for injuries consequent upon” federal officials’
violation of the Constitution).
The Constitution’s text expressly protects
fundamental rights but says little about the legal
remedies available for their violation.  That reflects
the fact that the Constitution was “layered on top” of
an existing “common law tradition” designed to hold
government officers accountable for committing legal
wrongs.  Stephen E. Sachs, Constitutional Backdrops,
80 Geo. Wash. L. Rev. 1813, 1822 (2012).  Th is legal
backdrop against which the Constitution was drafted,
debated, and ratified ensures that “[n]o man in this
country is so high that he is above the law.  No officer
of the law may set that law at defiance with impunity.
All the officers of the government, from the highest to
the lowest, are creatures of the law and are bound to
obey it.”  United States v. Lee, 106 U.S. 196, 220 (1882).
Because the Constitution was drafted against this
background common -law principle of officer
accountability, federal officers, including prison
officials, “are amenable for their injurious acts to the

3

judicial tribunals of the country, at the suit of the
oppressed.”  2 Joseph Story, Commentaries on the
Constitution of the United States § 1676, at 508 (3d ed.
1858).  Such suits for damages against federal officers
have been  a fundamental part of “our constitutional
system since the dawn of the Republic.”  Tanzin v.
Tanvir, 592 U.S. 43, 52 (2020).  When courts entertain
damages suits against federal officers who have
allegedly violated the Constitution, they do not intrude
upon Congress’s legislative power.  Instead, they
provide an important check on federal -government
action and ensure  judicial redress for abuse of
authority by federal officers as contemplated by the
Constitution.
Two precepts embedded in the Constitution’s text
and history support permitting an action here.  First,
when the Framers wrote the Constitution, they gave
the federal judiciary a critical role in our system of
separated powers.  As drafted, Article III establish ed
a federal judiciary with broad authority to enforce the
Constitution’s limitations on the power of government
in cases and controversies that come before the federal
courts.  Article III courts thus perform an essential
checking function on the political branches of
government, ensuring fidelity to the Constitution’s
structure and its guarantee of individual rights.
The Framers understood that constitutional
“[l]imitations . . . can be preserved in practice no other
way than through the medium of courts of justice,
whose duty it must be to declare all acts contrary to
the manifest tenor of the Constitution void.  Without
this, all the reservations of particular rights or
privileges would amount to nothing.”  The Federalist
No. 78, at 466 (Alexander Hamilton) (Clinton Rossiter
ed., 1961).  In the Framers’ constitutional design,
when other branches transgress the Constitution’s

4

limits, “the judicial department is a constitutional
check.”  2 The Debates in the Several State Conventions
on the Adoption of the Federal Constitution  196
(Jonathan Elliot ed., 1836) [hereinafter Elliot’s
Debates].
Second, and related to the first, the Framers wrote
Article III to ensure that where there is a legal right,
there is also a legal remedy for violation of that right.
The Framers drafted the Constitution against the
backdrop of English common law, and they understood
that legal rights were meaningless without the ability
to go to court to obtain a remedy when those rights
were violated.  As this Court recognized in Marbury v.
Madison, “it is a general and indisputable rule, that
where there is a legal right, there is also a legal
remedy[,] by suit or action at law, whenever that right
is invaded.”  5 U.S. (1 Cranch) 137, 163 (1803) (quoting
3 William Blackstone,  Commentaries *23).  Marbury
affirmed that “[t]he very essence of civil liberty
certainly consists in the right of every individual to
claim the protection of the laws, whenever he receives
an injury.”  Id.
As the states debated ratification, concerns
emerged that the Constitution did not adequately limit
the government’s ability to punish, leaving room for
federal officials to abuse their power and impose
torture and barbarity without accountability.  In this
context, the Eighth Amendment was drafted and
ratified to bar the federal government from inflicting
“cruel and unusual punishments.”  U.S. Const. amend.
VIII.
By the time of the Framing, p risons had long been
recognized as places where the threat of “cruel and
unusual punishments” was especially acute, whether
through intolerable conditions, abuse by prison
officials, or sheer neglect.  English law had responded

5

to this concern  by developing doctrines that
emphasized that a “prisoner is not to be punished in
gaol, but to be kept safely.”  R v. Huggins  (1730) 92
Eng. Rep. 518, 522 ; 2 Raym.  Ld. 1574, 1579  (K.B.).
These doctrines recognized that prison officials were
obliged to protect the health and safety of prisoners in
their care.  And they were enforced by English courts,
which held officials who abused their power to account
through fines, orders to change prison conditions,
removal from office, and even criminal prosecution.
See infra Section II.
Consistent with that history, this Court recognized
a half -century ago that prison officials’ deliberate
indifference to a prisoner’s serious medical need s
violates th e Eighth Amendment’s bar on cruel and
unusual punishment.  See Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S.
97, 104 (1976).  That is because such indifference can
cause prisoners “physical ‘torture,’” one of the “evils of
most immediate concern” to the Eighth Amendment’s
drafters.  Id. at 103 (quoting In re Kemmler, 136 U.S.
436, 447 (1890)); see Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825,
828 (1994).  Following that recognition, this Court held
in Carlson v. Green  “that the Eighth Amendment
Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause gave [federal
prisoners] a damages remedy for failure to provide
adequate medical treatment.”  Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 131.
Carlson confirmed that Bivens claims “directly under
the Constitution” are available in the prison context to
remedy exactly the harm Watanabe experienced —
Nielsen’s unconstitutional deliberate indifference to
his serious bodily injuries.  Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S.
14, 16-18 (1980).
Thus, although this Court has been reluctant to
extend Bivens to “any new context or new category of
defendants,” Ziglar, 582 U.S.  at 135 (quoting Corr.
Servs. Corp. v. Malesko , 534 U.S. 61, 68 (2001)) , this

6

case falls squarely within the context  this Court
already recognized and approved in Carlson: federal
prison officials’ violation of the Eighth Amendment’s
ban on deliberate indifference to a serious medical
need.  Indeed, even as this Court has declined to
extend Bivens to new contexts , it has continued to
acknowledge the existence of liability under Carlson.
See Ziglar, 582 U.S. at 131; Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S.
482, 490-91 (2022).  It should do so again in this case.
ARGUMENT
I. Under Article III, Federal Courts Can Grant
Relief When Government Officials Violate
Constitutional Rights.
A. Article III’s Text and History Make Clear
that Federal Courts  Have Broad Power
to Protect Constitutional Rights and
Prevent Abuse of Power by the
Government.
Article III of the Constitution broadly extends the
“judicial Power” to nine categories of cases and
controversies, including “all Cases, in Law and Equity,
arising under this Constitution, the Laws of the
United States, and Treaties made, or which shall b e
made, under their Authority.”  U.S. Const. art. III, § 2,
cl. 1.  Article III’s plain language empowers the
“judicial department” to “decide all cases of every
description, arising under the constitution or laws of
the United States,” obliging federal courts to “decid[e]
every judicial question which grows out of the
constitution and laws.”  Cohens v. Virginia, 19 U.S. (6
Wheat.) 264, 382, 384 (1821).
The Constitution’s sweeping grant of judicial power
to the newly created federal courts was a direct
response to one of the infirmities of the Articles of
Confederation, which established a single branch of

7

the federal government and no independent court
system.  See Akhil Reed Amar, Of Sovereignty and
Federalism, 96 Yale L.J. 1425, 1443 (1987) (explaining
that Confederation courts were “pitiful creatures of
Congress, dependent on its pleasure for their place,
tenure, salary, and power”).  Under the dysfunctional
Confederation government, individuals could not go to
court to enforce federal legal protections, prompting
Alexander Hamilton to observe that “[l]aws are a dead
letter without courts to expound and define their true
meaning and operation.”  The Federalist No. 22, supra,
at 150 (Alexander Hamilton).
The Framers recognized that “there ought always
to be a constitutional method of giving efficacy to
constitutional provisions.   What, for instance, would
avail restrictions on the authority of the State
legislatures, without some constitutional mode of
enforcing the observance of them? . . .  No man of sense
will believe that such prohibitions would be
scrupulously regarded without some effectual power in
the government to restrain or correct the infractions of
them.”  The Federalist No . 80 , supra, at 475 -76
(Alexander Hamilton).
At the Philadelphia Convention, the Framers
debated different mechanisms for ensuring compliance
with the Constitution.  As the Convention unfolded,
the Framers chose judicial review as a robust
constitutional check designed to preserve liberty and
guarantee constitutional accountability.  Although the
judiciary would not have “the sword or the purse,” The
Federalist No. 78, supra, at 465 (Alexander Hamilton),
it would retain broad powers to enforce constitutional
limitations and to maintain the rule of law by
adjudicating cases and controversies.
Over the course of the Convention, the Framers
expanded the federal courts’ jurisdiction to ensure that

8

the Article III judiciary would be “competent to the
decision of all questions arising out of the
constitution,” 4 Elliot’s Debates , supra, at 156, and
federal laws, giving the federal courts the power to
decide “all questions arising upon their construction,
and in a judicial manner to carry those laws into
execution,” Luther Martin, The Genuine Information,
Delivered to the Legislature of the State of Maryland,
Relative to the Proceedings of the General Convention
(Nov. 29, 1787), reprinted in  3 The Records of the
Federal Convention of 1787, at 172, 220 (Max Farrand
ed., 1911).
In the ensuing debates over ratification,
Federalists and Anti -Federalists alike agreed that
Article III gave the federal courts broad powers to
enforce the Constitution’s limits on the power of
government.  In the state s’ ratifying conventions, the
Constitution’s supporters repeatedly argued that the
judiciary would provide a critical check on the political
branches by guaranteeing individual rights and
ensuring compliance with the Constitution’s structure.
At the Virginia ratifying convention, John
Marshall proclaimed, “[t]o what quarter will you look
for protection from an infringement on the
Constitution, if you will not give the power to the
judiciary?  There is no other body that can afford such
a protection.”  3 Elliot’s Debates, supra, at 554.  James
Madison explained the Constitution’s “new policy” of
submitting constitutional questions to the “judiciary of
the United States”: “[t]hat causes of a federal nature
will arise, will be obvious to every gentleman who will
recollect that the states are laid under restrictions,
and that the rights of the Union are secured by these
restrictions.”  Id. at 532.  At the North Carolina
ratifying convention, Richard Dobbs Spaight insisted
that “if any man [i]s injured by an officer of the United

9

States, he could get redress by a suit at law.”  4 id. at
37.
Anti-Federalists complained bitterly about Article
III’s breadth, insisting that “[t]he jurisdiction of all
cases arising under the Constitution and the laws of
the Union is of stupendous magnitude.”  3 id. at 565.
But those arguments did not carry the day.  The state
conventions rejected Anti -Federalist claims that the
judicial power conferred in Article III was too broad
and ratified the Constitution, giving the newly created
federal courts sweeping judicial power to ensure that
“the Constitution should be carried into effect, that the
laws should be executed, justice equally done to all the
community, and treaties observed.”  4 id. at 160.  The
American people  thus recognized that “[t]hese ends
can only be accomplished by a general, paramount
judiciary.”  Id.
In 1789, when the Bill of Rights was added to the
Constitution, the Framers reaffirmed the role of the
federal courts in ensuring that the government would
respect constitutional limitations.  Introducing the Bill
of Rights in Congress, James Madison observed that if
it were “incorporated into the constitution,
independent tribunals of justice will consider
themselves in a peculiar manner the guardians of
those rights.”  1 Annals of Cong.  457 (1789) (Joseph
Gales ed., 1834).  “[T]hey will be an impenetrable
bulwark against every assumption of power in the
legislative or executive,” he continued, and “they will
be naturally led to resist every encroachment upon
rights expressly stipulated for in the constitution by
the declaration of rights.”  Id.
Madison recognized that “causes of a federal
nature” will arise under those provisions of the
Constitution in which “states are laid under
restrictions,” 3 Elliot’s Debates , supra, at 532, and

10

insisted that the federal courts would be obliged to
enforce the rights laid out in the Bill of Rights in cases
that came before them.  Judicial review was the key to
ensuring that the guarantees of the Bill of Rights were
not “paper barriers .  . . too weak to be worthy of
attention,” but rather real, enforceable limits on the
power of the federal government .  1 Annals of Cong. ,
supra, at 455.
In creating an independent federal judiciary with
the power to enforce constitutional limitations and
maintain the rule of law, the Framers incorporated
longstanding common-law principles that allowed
courts to vindicate individual rights, as the next
Section discusses.
B. The Framers Wrote Article III to Ensure
that Where a Legal Right Exists, so Does
a Legal Remedy for that Right’s
Infringement.
The Constitution was written, debated, and ratified
against a legal landscape that held federal officers
accountable for violating constitutionally guaranteed
rights.  See Andrew Kent, Lessons for  Bivens and
Qualified Immunity Debates from Nineteenth-Century
Damages Litigation Against Federal Officers, 96 Notre
Dame L. Rev. 1755, 1758 (2021) (“[T]he Framers and
ratifiers of the Constitution in 1787 -88 expected that
common law or general law would supply forms of
action to contest many kinds of misconduct by federal
officers.” (footnote omitted) ); Richard H. Fallon, Jr.,
Bidding Farewell to Constitutional Torts, 107 Calif. L.
Rev. 933, 942 -43 (2019). (“When harmed by official
misconduct at the dawn of constitutional history,
aggrieved parties could normally seek redress by
invoking forms of action available at common law and
in equity that included suits against governmental
officials under ordinary tort law.”).  The Framers, who

11

recognized that a legal right is meaningless if
individuals lack the ability to go to court and obtain a
remedy when it is violated, wrote Article III to ensure
that such legal remedies would be available under the
new constitutional structure they created.
Steeped in the writings of William Blackstone, the
Framers understood that rights and remedies must go
hand in hand if courts are to play their essential role
in the Constitution’s system of separat ed powers:
expounding the law and vindicating individual liberty.
See The Federalist  No. 43 , supra, at 274  (James
Madison) (“[A] right implies a remedy.”).  As
Blackstone had written, it was a “general and
indisputable rule, that where there is a legal right
there is also a legal remedy, by suit or action at law,
whenever that right is invaded.”  3 Blackstone,
Commentaries *23.  “[I]n vain would rights be
declared, in vain directed to be observed,” Blackstone
explained, “if there were no method of recovering and
asserting those rights, when wrongfully withheld or
invaded.  This is what we mean properly, when we
speak of the pro tection of the law.”  1 id. at *56; see
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins , 578 U.S. 330, 344 (2016)
(Thomas, J., concurring) (“Historically, common -law
courts possessed broad power to adjudicate suits
involving the alleged violation of private rights, even
when plaintiffs alleged only the violation of those
rights and nothing more.”); TransUnion LLC v.
Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413, 448 (2021) (Thomas, J.,
dissenting) ( “The principle that the violation of an
individual right gives rise to an actionable harm was
widespread at the founding.”).
These fundamental rule -of-law values were
affirmed by Founding -era state constitutions that
guaranteed redress for violations of legal rights.  The
Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 , for example,

12

provided that “[e]very subject  . . . ought to find a
certain remedy, by having recourse to the laws, for all
injuries or wrongs which he may receive in his person,
property, or character.”  Mass. Const. art. XI.  It
further elaborated on that principle, declaring that
“[h]e ought to obtain right and justice freely, and
without being obliged to purchase it; completely, and
without any denial; promptly, and without delay,
conformably to the laws.”  Id.  Other state
constitutions used similar formulations to protect the
right of individuals to seek redress in court for
violations of their legal rights.  See, e.g. , Md.
Declaration of Rts . of 1776, art. XVII; N.H. Const. of
1784, pt. 1, art. XIV; Vt. Const. of 1786, ch. 1, art. IV;
Pa. Const. of 1790, art. IX, §  11; Del. Const. of 1792,
art. I, §  9; Ky. Const. of 1792, art. XII, §  13; Tenn.
Const. of 1796, art. XI, § 17.
In Marbury v. Madison , Chief Justice Marshall
recognized that the federal Constitution also secured
these fundamental principles.  Under Article III, h e
explained, the “province of the court is, solely, to decide
on the rights of individuals,” and he invoked
Blackstone’s discussion of common-law principles that
ensure that “every right, when withheld, must have a
remedy, and every injury its proper redress.”
Marbury, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) at 163, 170 (quoting in part
3 Blackstone, supra, at *109).  As Marbury observed, a
broad understanding of the individual’s right to go to
court to redress violations of personal rights was
necessary to secure both “[t]he very essence of civil
liberty”—“the right of every individual to claim the
protection of the laws, whenever he receives an
injury”—and the Constitution’s promise of a
“government of laws, and not of men.”  Id. at 163.
“From the earliest years of the Republic, th [is]
Court has recognized the power of the Judiciary to

13

award appropriate remedies to redress injuries
actionable in federal court .”  Franklin v. Gwinnett
Cnty. Pub. Schs., 503 U.S. 60, 66 (1992).  In Marbury,
it did not matter that federal law did not grant an
express right of action to Marbury, nor even that “the
mandamus, now moved for, is not for the performance
of an act expressly enjoined by statute.”  Marbury, 5
U.S. (1 Cranch) at 172.  Because the refusal to deliver
Marbury’s commission violated his individual right to
the office, he had “a right to resort to the laws of his
country for a remedy.”  Id. at 166 ; see id. at 16 7
(explaining that such suits are “examinable in a
court”).  For more than two centuries  since, the
“historic judicial authority to award appropriate relief
. . . has been thought necessary to provide an
important safeguard against abuses of legislative and
executive power ” and “ to ensure an independent
Judiciary.”  Franklin, 503 U.S. at 74; see Martin v.
Hunter’s Lessee , 14 U.S. (1 Wheat.) 304, 350 (1816)
(rejecting a construction of Article III that “would, in
many cases,” result in “rights without corresponding
remedies”); Kendall v. United States ex  rel. Stokes, 37
U.S. (12 Pet.) 524, 624 (1838) (explaining that it would
be a “monstrous absurdity in a well organized
government, that there should be no remedy, although
a clear and undeniable right should be shown to
exist”).
II. The Eighth Amendment W as Adopted to
Guard Against a Government that Cou ld
Punish Without Limits.
The absence of a Bill of Rights in the original
Constitution launched an avalanche of criticism, as
many insisted that the Constitution was deficient
without guarantees for substantive individual rights
essential to liberty.   Among the rights that the
Founding generation sought to safeguard in a Bill of

14

Rights was protection against the political branches’
power to engage in abusive punishment, including of
those in government custody.  Indeed, by the time of
the Founding, the notion that government had to
protect individuals in its custody had deeply
established roots in English law.
 1.  At the time of the Framing, it was commonly
accepted that prisons presented a particular risk of
abusive punishment.  To begin, prisoners were
uniquely vulnerable; while in custody, they depend ed
on prison officials because they were in a position
where they “cannot help [themselves].”   Huggins, 92
Eng. Rep. at 522.  Prison officials, presented with that
vulnerability, were viewed as a “merciless race of
men,” warranting an “extraordinary anxiety of our law
in favour of prisoners.”  William Eden, Principles of
Penal Law 47 (1771).  And absent “attention” and
oversight, prisons inevitably degrade d in their ability
to “secur[e] the prisoners; and preserv[e] good order,
cleanliness.”  John Howard, The State of the Prisons in
England and Wales 33 (1777); see id. at 34 (noting that
prisons outside magistrates’ control were “more apt to
abuse their prisoners” in “shocking” and
“torment[ing]” ways).  Prisons were thus viewed as
fertile ground for “secret tyranny.”  Eden, supra, at 47.
Consistent with  that understanding, English law
recognized a pair of linked principles: “A prisoner is
not to be punished in gaol, but to be kept safely.”
Huggins, 92 Eng. Rep. at 522.
First, prisons could not inflict punishment above
that imposed by incarceration itself (through, for
example, poor conditions or jailer misconduct).  Prison
officials had to maintain a basic level of health and
safety, “lest the necessary miseries of a gaol be
aggravated by the unrestrained cruelty of the gaoler.”
Eden, supra, at 46.  “The laws of England do not suffer

15

private executions.  No condemned malefactor may be
secretly put to death; nor murdered in a prison directly
or indirectly: much less ought those to be destroyed
there whose sentence does not affect their life.”
Howard, supra, at 38; see id. at 17 & n.* (lamenting
that more prisoners were “destroyed” by gaol fever
“than were put to death by all the public executions in
the kingdom”). 2  Writing later, physician W.A. Guy
recounted the “gaol fever, the small -pox, and other
fatal maladies, which decimated our prisons less than
a century ago” and imposed “punishment” on
eighteenth-century prisoners “beyond that which the
law award[ed].”  W.A. Guy, On Some Results of a
Recent Census of the Population of the Convict Prisons
in England (1862), reprinted in 4 Nineteenth-Century
Crime and Punishment  101, 114 (Victor Bailey ed. ,
2022).
Second, prison officials had a duty to protect
prisoners.  A 1730 case, R v. Huggins, concerned prison
officials’ criminal liability for the death of a prisoner
kept in unhygienic conditions  directly above the
“common sewer .”  Huggins, 92 Eng. Rep.  at 519.
Huggins recognized that prison officials owed
prisoners a “duty” of care that is violated when,

2 The risk of extralegal punishment was acute.  “Outbreaks of
gaol fever,” another name for typhus, were “common in the
1750s.”  J.S. Cockburn, A History of English Assizes 1558 -1714,
at 53 n.4 (1972).  The disease regularly killed hundreds of people
in prisons and beyond, including sitting judges and the Lord
Mayor of London.  See Howard, supra, at 1 7-19; Frederick
Willcocks, The Black Assizes in the West  1-2 (1884).  “Gaol -
Distemper” was “a national concern of no small importance,”
Howard, supra, at 20, and Parliament recognized the “fatal
Consequences of that Disorder, of which there has been, of late,
too much Experience,” Health of Prisoners Act 1774, 14 Geo. 3 c.
59.

16

through their conduct, a prisoner is “brought nearer to
death, and farther from life.”  Id. at 522.  If an official
fails to keep those in their care safe and healthy, “it is
a breach . . . of the trust which the law has reposed in
him.”  Id.  Similarly, the court in Castell v. Bambridge
& Corbet confirmed that prison officials act improperly
by putting  prisoners into environments with known
and dangerous health risks , like contagious disease .
See Castell v. Bambridge & Corbet (1730) 93 Eng. Rep.
894, 896; 2 Str. 854, 856 (K.B.) (noting that “appellees
would be guilty of murder” for putting a prisoner
somewhere “small pox was there,” such “that he
caught the small pox . . . and died thereof”).
When prison officials violated that duty of care ,
English law intervened.  Some courts levied fines
directly against offending prison officials, as in Lady
Broughton’s Case, where a prison keeper was found
guilty of “hard usage of the prisoners in a most
barbarous manner” and ultimately “fined one hundred
marks,” as well as “removed from her office.”  Lady
Broughton’s Case (1672) 83 Eng. Rep. 112, 112 -13;
Raym. T. 216, 216  (K.B.); see 4 Blackstone, supra, at
*140 (noting that “ negligence of public officers ,
entrusted with the administration of justice, [such] as
sheriffs . . . makes the offender liable to be fined; and
in very notorious cases will amount to a forfeiture of
his office”).  Courts also imposed orders on prison
officials to improve conditions.  See Case of the Prison
of the King’s Bench (1726) 93 Eng. Rep. 778, 778; 2 Str.
678, 678 (K.B.) (ordering those running a prison “in a
ruinous condition” “to put the prison in repair, which
[the court] said the proprietors were obliged to do,
upon pain of forfeiting their right”).  Other courts
imposed criminal liability on officials who mistreated
prisoners in their care.  See Huggins, 92 Eng. Rep. at
521 (“If a prisoner by duress of the gaoler comes to an

17

untimely end, it is murder.  It is not necessary, to make
it duress, that there should be actual strokes or
wounds.”); Michael Foster, Crown Law 321-22
(Michael Dodson ed., 3d ed. 1792) (explaining that “if
[a prisoner’s] death was owing to cruel and oppressive
usage on the part of the gaoler . . . it will be deemed
wilful murder” and describing the facts of Huggins and
Castell as “ enormous violations of the trust the law
reposeth in its ministers of justice ”); Eden, supra, at
47 (declaring murder if a prisoner dies from “severities
unnecessary to the safe custody”).
2.  The fact that the  Constitution did not protect
against government overreach that could result in
these and other abuses caused considerable
controversy at the Founding.  Anti-Federalists
lamented that, absent a Bill of Rights, “[t]he officers of
Congress may come upon you now, fortified with all
the terrors of paramount federal authority.”  3 Elliot’s
Debates, supra, at 448.  Those who fought to add the
Bill of Rights  to the Constitution emphasized  federal
courts’ role in checking overreach by government
officials.  Civil damages actions, they understood, were
critical to prevent the federal government’s abuse of
power.
 One Anti-Federalist essayist explained the
constitutional checking function such damages
perform.  “[N]o remedy has been yet found equal to the
task of deter[r]ing and curbing the insolence of office,
but a jury” because “[i]t has become an invariable
maxim of English juries, to give ruinous damages
whenever an officer has deviated from the rigid let ter
of the law, or been guilty of an unnecessary act of
insolence or oppression. ”  Essays by  A Farmer, Md.
Gazette, Feb.-Apr. 1788, reprinted in 5 The Complete
Anti-Federalist 5, 14 (Herbert J. Storing ed., 1981) .
Likewise, Luther Martin emphasized that “jury

18

trials”—“the surest barrier against arbitrary power,
and the palladium of liberty”—were “most essential for
our liberty . . . in every case . . . between government
and its officers on the one part, and the subject or
citizen on the other.”  Martin, supra, at 221 -22
(emphasis omitted).  To the Founding generation, “the
right to trial by jury” was “‘the heart and lungs, the
mainspring and the center wheel’ of our liberties,
without which ‘the body must die; the watch must run
down; the government must become arbitra ry.’”
United States v. Haymond, 588 U.S. 634, 640-41 (2019)
(plurality opinion) (quoting Letter from Clarendon to
W. Pym (Jan. 27, 1766), in 1 Papers of John Adams
169 (R. Taylor ed., 1977)).
In Massachusetts, the Anti -Federalist essayist
Hampden insisted that “without [a jury], in civil
actions, no relief can be had against the High Officers
of State, for abuse of private citizens.”  Essays by
Hampden, Mass. Centinel, Jan.-Feb. 1788, reprinted
in 4 The Complete Anti-Federalist, supra, at 198, 200.
And during debates in Pennsylvania in 1787, another
writer argued that if “a constable, having a warrant to
search for stolen goods, pulled down the clothes of a
bed in which there was a woman, and searched under
her shift .  . . a trial by jury would be our safest
resource” because “heavy damages would at once
punish the offender, and deter others from committing
the same.”  Essay of A Democratic Federalist , Pa.
Herald, Oct. 17, 1787, reprinted in 3 The Complete
Anti-Federalist, supra, at 58, 61.
As the states debated ratification, there was
grave concern about the possibility of unlimited
government power , including the political branches’
power to punish.  In Massachusetts, Abraham Holmes
worried that the Constitution gave Congress full
power to decide “what kind of punishments shall be

19

inflicted on persons convicted of crimes” and “nowhere
restrained” the government from “inventing the most
cruel and unheard -of punishments, and annexing
them to crimes .”  2 Elliot’s Debates , supra, at 111.
Absent a “constitutional check,” “ racks and gibbets
may be amongst the most mild instruments” of federal
punishment.  Id.
In Virginia, Patrick Henry emphasized that “no
latitude ought to be left” to the federal government in
determining appropriate punishment s.  3  id. at 447.
Quoting the Virginia Declaration of Rights’ own ban
on cruel and unusual punishment, he decried the
power to “define punishments without this control,”
which would “let [federal officials] loose” and “depart
from the genius of your country.”  Id.  Henry stressed
that, absent a bar like Virginia’s, the Constitution
would “strengthen[] the arm of government” and
permit “tortures, or cruel and barbarous punishment,”
such that federal officials might “punish with still
more relentless severity” and le ave the American
people “lost and undone.”  Id. at 447-48.  George Mason
agreed, noting that directly limiting the government’s
power to punish served to “prohibit torture.”  See id. at
452; cf. 1 Annals of Cong. , supra, at  782-83 (Rep.
Livermore) (objecting to the proposed amendment on
grounds that it would “restrain[]” the infliction of
severe punishments like mutilation).
These concerns motivated the adoption of the
Eighth Amendment as part of the Bill of Rights, which
was added to  the Constitution  to establish broad
protections “indispensable to the full enjoyment of the
rights of personal security, personal liberty, and
private property.”  3 Joseph Story, Commentaries on
the Constitution of the United States  § 1895, at 748
(1833).  Drawing on similar restrictions in the 1689
English Bill of Rights, see 1 W. & M ., Sess. 2, c. 2

20

(1689); 4 Blackstone , supra, at  *378, the Virginia
Declaration of Rights, see Va. Declaration of Rts . of
1776, § 9, and other governing documents, the
Amendment barred the government from inflicting
“cruel and unusual punishments.”  U.S. Const. amend.
VIII.3
The Amendment ’s text  cabins government
discretion and forms a bulwark against federal
officials “let[ting] . . . loose” and inflicting “barbarous”
punishment, 3 Elliot’s Debates , supra, at 447 ,
including neglecting prisoners’ serious medical needs,
see Gamble, 429 U.S. at 103-04; Farmer, 511 U.S. at
828.  As this Court has recognized, p risoners “must
rely on prison authorities to treat [their] medical
needs.”  Gamble, 429 U.S. at 103.  Indeed, if
“authorities fail to do so, those needs will not be met,”
which can “produce physical ‘torture or a lingering
death,’ the evils of most immediate concern” to the
Eighth Amendment’s drafters.  Id. at 103 (quoting In
re Kemmler , 136 U.S. at 447).  Th is Court has
“therefore conclude[d] that deliberate indifference to
serious medical needs of prisoners constitutes the
‘unnecessary and wanton infliction of pain’ proscribed
by the Eighth Amendment.”  Id. at 104 (quoting Gregg
v. Georgia , 428 U.S. 153, 173 (1976)  (plurality

Barbarous or cruell.”); see also Anthony F. Granucci, “Nor Cruel

opinion)).  According to the Court, this conclusion was
grounded in the “common-law view that ‘[i]t is but just
that the public be required to care for the prisoner,
who cannot [,] by reason of the deprivation of his
liberty, care for himself.’”  Id. at 103-04 (quoting Spicer
v. Williamson , 132 S.E. 291, 293 (N.C . 1926)) ; see
South v. Maryland ex rel. Pottle, 59 U.S. (18 How.) 396,
402 (1855) (explaining that a sheriff, in his
“ministerial capacity,” “is keeper of the county jail, and
answerable for the safe -keeping of prisoners” ); cf.
Logan v. United States , 144 U.S. 263, 284 (1892)
(describing the federal government’s “ duty to protect
[pretrial prisoners], while so held, against assault or

III. Bivens and Carlson Properly Reflect
Longstanding Judicial Practice.
A. Courts in the Founding Generation
Vindicated Core Rights by Granting
Damages in Common-Law Tort Suits.
Early Americans courts vindicated constitutional
rights through common-law tort actions for damages.
“In the early Republic, ‘an array of writs .  . . allowed
individuals to test the legality of government conduct
by filing suit against government officials’ for money
damages ‘payable by the officer.’  These common -law
causes of action remained available through the 19th
century and into the 20th.”  Tanzin, 592 U.S.  at 49
(alteration in original) (quoting James E. Pfander &
Jonathan L. Hunt, Public Wrongs and Private Bills:
Indemnification and Government Accountability in the
Early Republic , 85 N.Y.U. L. Rev. 1862, 1871 -75
(2010)); see Ann Woolhandler, Patterns of Official
Immunity and Accountability , 37 Case W. R srv. L.
Rev. 396, 399 (1987) (“The predominant method of
suing officers in the early nineteenth century was an
allegation of common law harm, particularly a

22

physical trespass.  The issue of whether the action was
authorized by existing statutory or constitutional law
was introduced by way of defense and reply when the
officer pleaded justification.”).  Congress might choose
to indemnify the officer after the f act, but it was the
responsibility of courts in the first instance to uphold
the rule of law by holding a federal officer accountable
for violating the plaintiff’s rights.  See Pfander & Hunt,
supra, at 1868.
“[T]his exact remedy has coexisted with our
constitutional system since the dawn of the Republic,”
Tanzin, 592 U.S. at 52 , without requiring an express
legislative cause of action.  Indeed, from the Founding
on, this Court has permitted damages awards against
federal officers under nonstatutory common -law
claims.  See, e.g., Little v. Barreme, 6 U.S. (2 Cranch)
170, 179 (1804) (holding that a federal officer who
seized a Danish vessel “must be answerable in
damages”); Wise v. Withers, 7 U.S. (3 Cranch) 331, 332,
337 (1806) (permitting damages for an illegal intrusion
and seizure where the offending “court and the officer
are all trespassers”); Mitchell v. Harmony, 54 U.S. (13
How.) 115, 129-30, 137 (1852) (affirming a jury verdict
against a U.S. army officer for an “illegal act”) .  Thus,
“[a]t the Founding, and for much of American history,
there was no question as to whether federal courts had
the power to provide judge -made damages remedies
against individual federal officers.  Not only did
federal courts routinely provide such relief, but t he
Supreme Court repeatedly blessed the practice.”
Stephen I. Vladeck, The Disingenuous Demise and
Death of Bivens, 2019 -2020 Cato Sup. Ct. Rev. 263,
267 (2020).
In short, Petitioner’s insistence that judge -made
remedies have no place in our constitutional system is
belied by  constitutional history.   Founding-era

23

principles establishing that “[n]o officer of the law may
set that law at defiance with impunity,” Lee, 106 U.S.
at 220, are deeply rooted in this Court’s case law, see,
e.g., Bates v. Clark, 95 U.S. 204, 209 (1877); Belknap v.
Schild, 161 U.S. 10, 19 (1896); Phila. Co. v. Stimson ,
223 U.S. 605, 619 -20 (1912)  (“The exemption of the
United States from suit does not protect its officers
from personal liability to persons whose rights . . . they
have wrongfully invaded.”) ; Butz v. Economou , 438
U.S. 478, 489 -90 (1978)  (“[A] federal official was
protected for action tortious under state law only if his
acts were authorized by controlling federal law.”), and
form the backdrop for this Court’s decisions permitting
relief in Bivens and Carlson.
B. Bivens-Carlson Actions Are Proper
Where Federal Prison Officials Violate
Prisoners’ Constitutional Rights.
Consistent with both the Constitution’s text and
history and the tradition of common -law actions for
unlawful conduct by federal officers, this Court held in
Bivens that “damages may be obtained for injuries
consequent upon a violation of the [Constitution] by
federal officials.”  Bivens, 403 U.S. at 395.  As this
Court explained, “damages have been regarded as the
ordinary remedy for an invasion of personal interests
in liberty.”  Id.; see Bush v. Lucas , 462 U.S. 367, 378
(1983) ( observing that, under Bivens, “[t]he federal
courts’ statutory jurisdiction to decide federal
questions confers adequate power to award damages
to the victim of a constitutional violation”).  Under
these Founding-era principles , “the judiciary has a
particular responsibility to assure the vindication of
constitutional interests,” Bivens, 403 U.S. at 407
(Harlan, J., concurring in the judgment), and “‘rights’
and ‘remedies’” are “link[ed]” in “a 1:1 correlation,” id.
at 400 n.3 (citing Marbury, 5 U.S. (1 Cranch) at 163).

24

Under Bivens, when federal law supplies a basis
for jurisdiction and “some form of damages is the only
possible remedy,” id. at 409, “a traditional judicial
remedy such as damages is appropriate to the
vindication of the personal interests protected” by the
Constitution, id. at 399.  Such claims are entirely
compatible with this Court’s decision in Erie Railroad
Co. v. Tompkins, which excluded “matters governed by
the Federal Constitution” from its landmark rejection
of “federal general common law.”   304 U.S. 64, 78
(1938); see Henry J. Friendly, In Praise of Erie—and
the New Federal Common Law, 39 N.Y.U. L. Rev. 383,
405 (1964) (arguing that Erie permits the development
of a uniform “specialized federal common law” in
“areas of national concern”  (emphasis added) ).  In
Carlson v. Green , this Court applied Bivens in the
federal-prison context, rejecting suggestions that
“judicially created remedies” against federal prison
staff were “inappropriate” under “our constitutional
scheme” and expressly recognizing that such remedies
“directly under the Constitution ” are available when
prison officials violate the Eighth Amendment.
Carlson, 446 U.S. at 16 & n.1, 19.
Bivens’s recognition of a freestanding federal claim
against federal officers coheres with the long tradition
of accountability for government overreach that was in
place when the Constitution was drafted and ratified.
Under that tradition, legal remedies were available for
abuse of power by federal law -enforcement officers.
Bivens (and, later, Carlson) ensured that tradition ’s
continued existence by recognizing a federal claim
against federal officers who violate the Constitution.
In so doing, they also protected federal officers from
being subjected to the vagaries of fifty different state
common-law regimes.  In any event, today a state
common-law suit is no longer available because the

25

1988 Westfall Act forecloses common -law tort suits
against federal officers.  See 28 U.S.C. §  2679(b)(1);
Minneci v. Pollard , 565 U.S. 118, 126 (2012).
Tellingly, the Westfall Act does permit suits against
federal employees for violation of constitutional rights,
see 28 U.S.C . § 2679(b)(2)(A), which this Court has
recognized as an “explicit exception for Bivens claims,”
Hui v. Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799, 807 (2010)—powerful
evidence that Congress has put its imprimatur behind
the Bivens cause of action.
Bivens reflects the Framers’ view that a civil
remedy is necessary to prevent individuals , including
prisoners, from being subjected to “all the terrors of
paramount federal authority.”  3 Elliot’s Debates ,
supra, at 448.  Otherwise, federal correctional officers
would have the untrammeled authority to subject
prisoners in federal custody to all manner of cruel and
unusual punishment, including deprivation s of
necessary medical care.  Prisoners are uniquely
vulnerable, and this Court has affirmed that “[w]hen a
prison regulation or practice offends a fundamental
constitutional guarantee, federal courts will discharge
their duty to protect constitutional rights.”  Procunier
v. Martinez, 416 U.S. 396, 405-06 (1974); see Valentine
v. Collier , 590 U.S. 935, 940 (2020) (Sotomayor, J.,
statement respecting the denial of application to
vacate stay ) (noting that prisoners are “often
powerless to protect themselves from harm”) ; cf.
Daniels v. Williams, 474 U.S. 327, 335 (1986) (“Jailers
may owe a special duty of care to those in their custody
under state tort law.”).
Such rights enforcement effectuates the judiciary’s
longstanding role in maintaining the rule of law and
the separation of powers, and “[c]ourts may not allow
constitutional violations to continue simply because a
remedy would involve intrusion into the realm of

26

prison administration.”  Brown v. Plata, 563 U.S. 493,
511 ( 2011); see id. (“Courts nevertheless must not
shrink from their obligation to ‘enforce the
constitutional rights of all “persons,” including
prisoners.’” (quoting Cruz v. Beto , 405 U.S. 319, 321
(1972) (per curiam)).
Watanabe’s suit against Nielsen falls squarely
within the core of Bivens as applied in Carlson.
Nielsen was deliberately indifferent to Watanabe’s
serious medical needs, refusing to send him to a
hospital or provide any  treatment for his “severe”
injuries beyond “over -the-counter pain medication .”
Pet. App. 2a, 4a.  Permitting this suit to proceed under
Carlson would neither fashion a new cause of action
nor break new Bivens ground, but simply confirm that
federal prison officials can be held accountable for
violating constitutionally guaranteed rights, as
constitutional text and history require.

27

CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the
court of appeals should be affirmed.
